subject: Bayesian hierarchical model: Unexpected strong shrinkage

messages.author: b8863e2cc3f8818f
messages.subject: Bayesian hierarchical model: Unexpected strong shrinkage
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I am currently working on estimating effects (let's say, of a genetic variant) in various subgroups (e.g.  ethnicity, regions, or disease, with > 15 groups)  using a Bayesian hierarchical model with uninformative priors:


\begin{align}
  y_i      &\sim N(\theta_i, \sigma_i^2)\\  
  \theta_i &\sim N(\mu, \tau^2) \\
  \sigma_i &\sim cauchy(0, 2 \times range_y) \\
  \mu      &\sim N(0, \tau^2) \\
  \tau     &= 100
\end{align}


I am trying to understand some unexpected results, which lead to extreme shrinkage across all subgroups compared to a fully stratified analysis in a specific dataset, giving very similar estimates and very similar credible intervals.

My current interpretation is that there a no differential effects/heterogeneity in the subgroups (e.g. Isquared~6%), and, therefore, the results are shrunken to the same estimate, comparable to a fixed effects model. However, I wonder why the credible intervals are of similar size, because the sample sizes and standard errors vary considerably in the fully stratified analysis. The variances of the prior distributions are large enough, so even larger values do not seem to affect the estimates or credible intervals.


My R/Stan code seems to be ok, since the results for the 8schools data set match other publications (Gelman, 2014, BDA3). However, in the 8schools results, heterogeneity is absent (Isquared=0%), but the shrinkage is much weaker (moderate) compared to the other model described above.


My questions:

1) What are factors influencing shrinkage (priors, overall effect size, number of subgroups, ..) which could explain these findings?
2) Are there criteria to evaluate whether the observed shrinkage is adequate?

3) Are there situations/data where a Bayesian hierarchical (shrinkage) model is not recommended?

 

Any comments are welcome!

 

Thanks in advance,

 

Wilmar
